title: EduWiki Hub OERs (August–November 2026): Open Resources for Critical Literacy and Better Teaching
content:
Between August and November 2026, the EduWiki Hub continued to grow its library of Open Educational Resources (OERs), thanks to educators, affiliate groups, and community volunteers who keep sharing what works in their classrooms and training sessions.

This latest round highlights nine contributions in English, Spanish, and Indonesian, another reminder of how multilingual the Wikimedia education community is. Seven of the resources are available in English, two in Spanish, and one in Indonesian. They come from Uruguay, Indonesia, Wikimedia España, the Open Knowledge Foundation, and Wikimedia UK.

Core Wikipedia Editing & Critical Literacy: The largest group this period, combining workshop slide decks and a practical search tool. They help educators introduce how Wikipedia works, guide first-time editors, and encourage learners to think critically about whose knowledge is represented. Contributed by Wikimedia UK and Wikimedia España, in English and Spanish.

title: From Abidjan with Knowledge Equity: Reflections on WikiIndaba 2026
content:
From 13-15 November 2026, African Wikimedians gathered in Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire, for the 10th edition of WikiIndaba under the theme Africa’s Future: Knowledge Equity and Innovation. After the cancellation of the planned 2025 edition, this gathering felt like a long-awaited reunion and a deliberate step forward.

Hosted by the Wikimedia Community User Group Côte d’Ivoire and coordinated with Wiscom, the conference brought together more than 200+ participants from roughly 40 countries and the diaspora, working in English, French, and Arabic. Parallel to the main program ran the WikiIndaba Hackathon, satellite events across the continent, and a pre-conference for African users with extended rights focused on “Beyond Editing.”

The energy in Abidjan was unmistakable. Sessions spanned equity and community health, GLAM and cultural heritage, research/education/technology, and movement governance. Conversations repeatedly returned to practical questions: how to close content and participation gaps in African languages, how to make tools more usable in low-connectivity environments, and how to document local knowledge so it is both visible and trusted globally.

title: Celebrating Wikidata’s 14th Birthday in Lafia, Nigeria: Bringing Community and Open Knowledge Together
content:
Wikidata turned 14 in October 2026, marking another year of making structured, freely accessible knowledge available to people around the world. From its beginnings as a collaborative knowledge base, Wikidata has grown into an important resource for Wikipedia, researchers, developers, cultural institutions and communities working to make information more accessible.

To mark this milestone, we brought the celebration to Lafia, the capital of Nasarawa State, Nigeria, through an in-person gathering that brought members of the local community together to celebrate Wikidata and the people who contribute to its growth.

For us, the occasion was more than a birthday party. It was an opportunity to connect people, strengthen interest in open knowledge and create more awareness about the role Wikidata can play in documenting the people, places, culture and heritage of Nigeria.

Of course, no birthday celebration would be complete without a cake!

We marked the occasion with a specially designed Wikidata birthday cake featuring the 14th birthday branding. It was a simple but memorable part of the gathering, giving everyone an opportunity to celebrate the project and the community behind it.

title: Wikidata and Wikisource Collaboration: Basic Wikidata Editing Training Focusing on Wikisource Manuscripts and Books
content:
Looking back at Saturday, August 22, 2026, introducing Wikidata to new contributors often comes with its own unique challenges. Unlike Wikipedia, which is familiar for its narrative paragraph format, Wikidata operates on structured data logic filled with item codes and statements. When taught abstractly, this concept can feel overwhelming for beginners.

Pijri Paijar, Dokumentasi WikiLatih Wikidata oleh Komunitas Wikisource Indonesia – 02, Wikimedia Indonesia, CC BY-SA 4.0

To bridge this gap, the Indonesian Wikisource Community, represented by Cgjkldn (lead trainer) and Pijri Paijar (activity coordinator), facilitated an online basic-level Wikidata WikiLatih using a more concrete approach: cataloging manuscripts and books available on Indonesian Wikisource. By using this digital collection of books and manuscripts as hands-on practice material, participants could directly see how a text already transcribed on Wikisource can be given a neat data identity and connected globally on Wikidata.

title: Who Gets to Shape the Future of AI? Bringing African Wiki Women into the Conversation
content:
Artificial intelligence is changing how we access information, create content, learn, and interact with the world. But as these technologies become increasingly influential, an important question deserves attention: Who gets to shape the future of AI, and whose perspectives are being considered?

For Africa, this is more than a technology question. It is about representation, language, access, and participation. African knowledge, cultural contexts, languages, and lived experiences are not always adequately represented in the information systems shaping the digital world. If AI is to serve diverse communities, those communities must have opportunities to contribute to the knowledge, discussions, and decisions influencing its development.

This is where open knowledge communities have an important role to play.

The Wikimedia movement has spent years building a global knowledge ecosystem through collaboration, free access to information, and community-led knowledge production.

title: What Stays After the Workshop: Western Armenian Wikipedia in Diaspora Schools
content:
In the summer of 2024, part of a Wikimedia Foundation grant went on 40 dollars of mobile data. Azniv Stepanian and I were running Wikipedia trainings in Beirut for Western Armenian speakers, as Beirut is one of the cradles of the language. Power and WiFi were unreliable, and the mobile data let participants work from our phones’ hotspots. In the week our team arrived, border clashes flared in southern Lebanon, a drone hit Beirut, and flights were suspended for several days. Several youth centers and scout groups we had lined up canceled at the last minute. We had planned for 250 participants; we trained 30, and ten went on to edit.

The part that worked was improvised. We collected the email addresses of people who could not come and guided some of them over WhatsApp and Google Meet until they started editing. Since then, we ask every education project the same question: what will still be there once we leave?

title: From Content Contributors to Technology Enablers: Empowering Regional Tulu-Kannada Wikimedia Communities
content:
What if a Wikipedia editor could become a data curator?
What if a Wikisource contributor could learn to automate digitization workflows?
What if a regional-language volunteer could build a tool that benefits an entire Wikimedia community?

This is the kind of transformation that happens when Wikimedia communities come together not just to create content, but to learn how the technology behind free knowledge works.

On 14–15 November 2026, the Karavali Wikimedians User Group brought this vision to life through the Wiki Loves Tuluvas – Knowledge Sharing Sessions 2026, a two-day technical capacity-building program held at the CEOL Incubation Centre in Mangalore, Karnataka, India.

The sessions brought together 11 participants from the Tulu and Kannada Wikimedia communities for an intensive journey into the technical side of the Wikimedia ecosystem. With guidance from resource person Anoop Rao, participants explored tools, platforms and workflows that can help regional communities become more confident, capable and self-reliant.

title: Contributing in a Language I Can’t Speak: What I Learned at the Japan-Korea Friendship Event in Ulsan
content:
Last week, as a continuation of the Japan-Korea friendship event in Karatsu held this September, where I was part of the organizing team, I took part in the 2026 Japan-Korea friendship event at Ulsan. We visited a wide range of places, from a library in Busan to the Ulsan Museum and Ulsan Castle.

The last time I was at Gimhae International Airport, two years ago, it was just a layover on my way to study abroad. Coming back two years later, and this time getting to see the world beyond the airport, meant a lot to me personally.

Of everything I experienced, one thing stood out: I was able to contribute to Wikimedia projects in a language I can’t speak fluently. In this post, I’d like to share how that happened, and what I learned along the way.

Until now, I had only worked on Wikimedia projects in Japanese, my native language, and English, which I became reasonably fluent in through self-study and studying abroad. Since I didn’t know any other languages, I assumed that was simply how it had to be.

title: Celebrating 14 Years of Wikidata: Learning, Creativity and Community Engagement in the Igbo Wikimedians User Group
content:
Wikidata’s 14th birthday celebration in the Igbo Wikimedians User Group began virtually on Friday, 16 October 2026, for our community members who are neither in Abuja nor Awka. The virtual celebration was fun as we reflected on our success, challenges, and the way forward. The highlight of the session was when community members’ knowledge of Wikidata and its sister projects was tested.

Following the virtual celebration, we gathered in-person at two locations: Godwin Art Gallery, Awka, Anambra State, and the Enspirehub, Merit House, Maitama, Abuja. The celebration brought together 55 participants for a day of learning, creativity, games, networking, and appreciation of the free knowledge movement. The event provided an opportunity for participants to explore Wikidata, understand its importance, and experience knowledge-sharing in a fun and interactive environment. It was facilitated by Senator Choko, Macocobovi, and King ChristLike.

title: Connecting Communities and Sharing Knowledge: My Experience at Wiki Indaba 2026 in Abidjan
content:
From 13 to 15 November 2026, I had the opportunity to participate in the Wiki Indaba 2026 conference in Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire. The conference brought together Wikimedians, language activists, open knowledge advocates, and representatives of Wikimedia communities from across Africa to share experiences, discuss challenges, and explore opportunities for strengthening the movement on the continent.

Representing the Dagbani Wikimedians User Group, I was particularly excited to meet fellow Wikimedians, learn from their experiences, and explore ideas that could contribute to the growth of our community and other Mabia language projects.

Our presentation highlighted the importance of protecting indigenous languages in the digital space and how Wikimedia projects provide opportunities to document, preserve, and promote the Dagbani language and cultural heritage.

We also shared the work, experiences, and achievements of the Dagbani Wikimedians User Group, including our efforts to make Dagbani knowledge accessible to a global audience.

content:

title: Even horse breeds are subject to human bias: here’s why
content:
Hello, I’m Tsaag Valren, and those who know me know that I mostly contribute to Wikipedia and Wikidata on the subject of horse breeds. I have already written about creating genealogical graphs and visualizing them on Wikidata. Perhaps that led you to believe that horse breeds are a 100% objective topic to contribute on?

Horse breeds are a subject heavily affected by human bias. We can start by asking this question: who decides that a horse breed is a horse breed? The concept of horse breed was forged in Italy, and later in England out of the breeding of the Thoroughbred in the 18th century. From there, you can guess that naturalists, English ones in particular, traveled all over the world to describe the “breeds” of other countries, even when locally nobody cared about the concept of breed. Sometimes, breeds are described in a way that matches the distinctions the riders and breeders of those countries make themselves. And sometimes, not at all!

title: Waali and Dagaare Wikimedians Communities Organised Wiki Loves Food 2026 PhotoWalk at Wa Market
content:
On Sunday, 15 November 2026, the Wali Wikimedians Community, in collaboration with the Dagaare Wikimedians Community, organised a PhotoWalk at the Wa Market in the Upper West Region of Ghana as part of the ongoing Wiki Loves Food 2026 international photography contest. The activity brought together members of both Wikimedia communities to document indigenous foods, traditional ingredients and the rich culinary heritage of the people of northern Ghana through photography.

Wiki Loves Food is an international Wikimedia photography contest that seeks to document food cultures, traditional dishes, local ingredients and culinary practices from different parts of the world. The 2026 edition runs for one month, from 1 November to 30 November 2026, providing participants with an opportunity to contribute photographs that showcase the diversity of food and culinary traditions across different communities. Through this initiative, photographs of local foods and ingredients can be uploaded to Wikimedia Commons, making them freely accessible for educational, cultural and informational purposes.

title: Building the tools that help Africa tell its own stories: PULA at the WikiIndaba Hackathon 2026
content:
Building the tools that help Africa tell its own stories matters as much as writing the stories themselves.

As large as Africa is, we have so many languages to be poetic 🙂 Every story is told in a language, and every language leaves its own words: how they are spelt, what they mean, and how they sound when a typical African grandma with that language’s accent says them.

With technology, our stories travel more and more. Search engines, translation tools and voice assistants add to this progress, but these tools can only speak the languages they have words for, so if our languages, the pronunciations, the words are missing from the data, our stories will be missing from everything built on top of it.

This brings us to solving the problem, or having someone who has to put those words and voices into the data with the help of a tool that will make it possible. I never imagined I would be amongst the people or be that “someone”, and, funny enough, my journey into becoming a part of these started with a lot of doubt.
snippet: Building the tools that help Africa tell its own stories matters as much as writing the stories themselves.
creator: Essa237

title: Tech News 2026 – Issue 48
content:
Latest tech news from the Wikimedia technical community. Please tell other users about these changes. Not all changes will affect you. Translations are available.

Updates for editors

  • Administrators can now block users from creating new pages in specific namespaces while still allowing them to edit existing pages in those namespaces. This provides a way to address repeated page creation policy violations without preventing otherwise constructive contributors from continuing to edit the wiki. [1]
  • The Reader Growth team is running an A/B test of semantic search (also known as natural language search) on the web version of Wikipedia. The test, which begins on English Wikipedia, allows users to search with natural-language queries rather than relying only on keywords and will run until mid-December. Users can try semantic search and are encouraged to report risks and edge cases on the project talk page. Keep &mpo=semantic-search-for-web:hybrid-srp at the end of the URL when performing multiple searches to see semantic results.

title: From Nairobi to Ouagadougou: What Happens When Computational Social Scientists Meet Wikipedians Across Africa
content:
Between June and August 2026, three computational social science summer schools tried something new. In Nairobi (Kenya), Uyo (Nigeria), and Ouagadougou (Burkina Faso), early-career researchers learned R (the data analysis programming language), network analysis, and machine learning as expected. But this time, local or regional Wikimedians attended to also show them how to use Wikipedia and Wikidata as datasets, not just as reference tools. 

Why did this happen? Traditionally, many computational social scientists have worked with data from commercial social networks: for example, previously Twitter offered very liberal access to its data via APIs, many researchers used it to evaluate social dynamics, public opinion, and political trends. Researchers have also studied Facebook and Reddit. Recently, commercial social networks have restricted access to their data, and consequently researchers struggle to find usable data sources. Thanks to their open data licenses and policies, the Wikimedia projects offer a rich ecosystem for study, but researchers often know less about them.
